message:
QUESTION:
Did guard X's three-point shooting genuinely improve after the mid-season change of shooting coach, and should X take a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season?

DATA:
Professional basketball. Guard X's shooting before and after a mid-season change of shooting coach, which took effect after game 30. X played in all 50 games. His minutes per game were similar in both periods (about 32).

Shooting percentage = makes / attempts.

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 |
| Three-point attempts | 150 | 80 |
| Three-point makes | 51 | 32 |
| Free-throw attempts | 100 | 70 |
| Free-throw makes | 80 | 55 |

League average three-point percentage this season: 36%.

Opponent breakdown: in games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 three-point attempts came in 4 games against the league's two worst-ranked perimeter defences, and he made 18 of those 30. X did not face either of those teams in games 1-30.

The coaching staff must decide whether to increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season. The new shooting coach worked with the whole squad, not just X.

<analysis>
# Guard X: Three-Point Shooting Since the Coaching Change

## Summary

The data do not show that X's three-point shooting genuinely improved after the change of shooting coach. They do not support giving him a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season.

His raw percentage rose from 34.0% to 40.0%, but three facts undercut that rise:

- **Weak opponents explain the gain.** The rise comes entirely from 30 attempts against the league's two weakest perimeter defences, teams he did not face before game 30. Against all other opponents he shot 28% after the change, below his pre-change rate.
- **The gap is within normal variation.** Even before adjusting for opponents, a 6-point difference on these sample sizes is easily produced by chance.
- **Free throws went the other way.** His free-throw percentage fell slightly (80.0% to 78.6%), so there is no corroborating sign of improved mechanics.

Over the full season X shot 36.1%, which is the league average. That is the best current estimate of his ability.

## Data and context

- The season is split at game 30, when the new shooting coach took over. The coach works with the whole squad, not only X.
- X played all 50 games, at about 32 minutes per game in both periods. Changes in playing time or injury therefore do not explain any difference.
- Shooting percentage = makes ÷ attempts.

| | Games 1–30 | Games 31–50 | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-point makes / attempts | 51 / 150 | 32 / 80 | 83 / 230 |
| Three-point % | 34.0% | 40.0% | 36.1% |
| Three-point attempts per game | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.6 |
| Free-throw makes / attempts | 80 / 100 | 55 / 70 | 135 / 170 |
| Free-throw % | 80.0% | 78.6% | 79.4% |

League average three-point percentage: 36%.

## 1. The headline improvement is driven by opponents

In games 31–50, 30 of X's 80 attempts came in 4 games against the two worst-ranked perimeter defences. He made 18 of them (60%). He did not play either team in games 1–30, so the two periods faced different opposition.

| Games 31–50 | Makes / attempts | % |
|---|---|---|
| vs two worst perimeter defences (4 games) | 18 / 30 | 60.0% |
| vs all other opponents (16 games) | 14 / 50 | 28.0% |
| Total | 32 / 80 | 40.0% |

Against the rest of the league, the opponents most comparable to his games 1–30 schedule, X shot 28%. That is 6 points worse than before the change, not better.

The 60% figure is itself only 30 shots over 4 games and should not be read as his true level against weak defences. Still, the split shows that the aggregate 40% is a schedule effect, not evidence of a better shooter.

## 2. Even the raw difference is within chance

Leave the opponent split aside. A rise from 34.0% (150 attempts) to 40.0% (80 attempts) has a standard error of roughly 6.7 percentage points. The observed 6-point gain is therefore under one standard error, well within what random variation produces.

A true 36% shooter would quite often post a 34% stretch followed by a 40% stretch over these sample sizes. Three-point percentage needs several hundred attempts before it stabilises, and the post-change sample is 80.

The 28% figure against other opponents is similarly noisy on 50 attempts. The honest conclusion is not that X got worse. It is that nothing in these data distinguishes his post-change shooting from his pre-change shooting, once opponents are accounted for.

## 3. Free throws do not corroborate a change in mechanics

The draft cited a free-throw rise from 80% to 86%. That is incorrect: 55 of 70 is **78.6%**, a slight decline. The change is also too small to mean anything on 70 attempts.

Free throws are a reasonable, if imperfect, check on shooting technique, because they are uncontested and taken from a fixed spot. If anything, they point away from a mechanical improvement.

## 4. Other points to note

- **Volume fell.** X went from 5.0 to 4.0 three-point attempts per game at the same minutes. Taking fewer, possibly more selective, shots can raise percentage without any change in skill. Larger volume next season would likely push his efficiency the other way.
- **The coach worked with the whole squad.** The team's own before-and-after three-point figures, split by opponent strength, would be a far better test of the coaching effect than one player's 80 attempts. If the whole team improved against comparable opponents, that would be meaningful evidence. If only X's numbers rose, and only against weak defences, that points to schedule and noise.
- **Expected value.** At his season rate of 36.1%, an X three is worth about 1.08 points per attempt, the same as a league-average three. There is no evidence yet that moving attempts from team-mates to X adds points. That depends on how team-mates compare, which these data do not show.

## Recommendation

1. **Do not increase X's share of team three-point attempts on the strength of this data.** Plan around him as a roughly league-average (about 36%) three-point shooter.
2. **Make the comparison that would actually answer the question.** This means opponent-adjusted three-point percentage before and after the change for X and the rest of the squad. Where tracking data exist, also compare shot quality: contested versus open, and catch-and-shoot versus off-the-dribble.
3. **Keep collecting evidence.** Continue X's work with the new coach. Reassess once he has a few hundred post-change attempts against a representative range of opponents.
4. **Set a decision trigger in advance.** For example, revisit his role if, after roughly 250–300 further attempts, his opponent-adjusted rate is clearly above league average. Do not reward or penalise him on short streaks in either direction.

---

### Main corrections to the draft

- **Free-throw percentage** fell from 80.0% to 78.6%; it did not rise to 86%. The "corroborating evidence" claim is therefore removed.
- **The opponent breakdown was ignored.** Against opponents other than the two weakest perimeter defences, X shot 28% (14 of 50) after the change.
- **Statistical uncertainty is added.** The 6-point raw gain is under one standard error. The original caveats treated sample size as a minor note rather than the central issue.
- **The full-season rate (36.1%, exactly league average)** is reported as the best estimate of X's ability.
- **The fall in attempts per game** is flagged as a possible shot-selection effect.
- **Whole-squad coaching** is used as an opportunity for a better comparison, rather than left as unexplained context.
- **The conclusion and recommendation are reversed** to match the evidence.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review: Guard X Three-Point Analysis

The analysis is sound. Every figure checks out, the conclusion follows from the evidence, and the recommendation fits the conclusion. My suggestions are mainly about presentation, plus two analytical points that would strengthen it.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Claimed | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| 3P% games 1–30 | 34.0% | 51/150 = 34.0% ✓ |
| 3P% games 31–50 | 40.0% | 32/80 = 40.0% ✓ |
| Season 3P% | 36.1% | 83/230 = 36.09% ✓ |
| vs weakest defences | 60.0% | 18/30 ✓ |
| vs all others | 28.0% | 14/50 ✓ |
| FT% | 80.0 / 78.6 / 79.4 | ✓ |
| Attempts per game | 5.0 / 4.0 / 4.6 | ✓ |
| SE of the difference | ~6.7 pp | √(.34·.66/150 + .40·.60/80) = 6.71 pp ✓ |
| Points per attempt | ~1.08 | 3 × 0.361 = 1.083 ✓ |

## What works well

- It puts the opponent split first. That is the most important fact in the data.
- It correctly says the 28% figure is also noise, rather than concluding that X got worse.
- It uses the whole-squad coaching to propose a better test.
- It sets a decision trigger in advance, which is good practice.

## Issues to fix

**1. Remove the references to a draft (most important).**
The section "Main corrections to the draft" and the sentence "The draft cited a free-throw rise from 80% to 86%…" in Section 3 refer to a document the reader has never seen. The coaching staff only need the corrected analysis. Cut the corrections list, and change Section 3 to state the finding directly: "Free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% to 78.6%…" If you want a change log, keep it as a separate note.

**2. The shot-selection explanation doesn't fit the split.**
Section 4 suggests lower volume might have raised his percentage through better shot selection. The split points the other way:

- Against the weakest defences he took about 7.5 attempts per game (30 in 4 games) and shot 60%.
- Against everyone else he took about 3.1 per game (50 in 16 games) and shot 28%.

Where he was most "selective", his percentage dropped. Either drop the point or reframe it: the drop in volume against normal opponents may mean defences were limiting his looks. Also soften "Larger volume next season would likely push his efficiency the other way". It's plausible, but these data don't show it.

**3. Say whether 36.1% is a fair or flattering baseline.**
Excluding the 30 attempts against the two weakest defences, X shot 65/200 = 32.5% for the season. Whether 36.1% or 32.5% is the right planning figure depends on how often he will face weak defences next season. Four games out of fifty may be a normal share, in which case 36.1% is reasonable. One sentence on this would make the recommendation more robust, and either figure supports "no increase".

**4. Make the decision trigger concrete.**
"Clearly above league average" after 250–300 attempts needs a number. At around 275 attempts the standard error is about 2.9 pp. So "clearly above" means roughly 40% or better against representative opponents. A threshold of 37–38% would still be within noise.

## Minor points

- "The rise comes entirely from…" is fair. "Weak opponents explain the gain" is slightly stronger than the data allow, since both effects are small-sample. "Is accounted for by" would be more precise.
- The "Data and context" section says changes in playing time or injury don't explain the difference. Equal minutes rule out playing time, but they don't fully rule out a minor injury. Suggest "playing time does not explain any difference."

## Verdict

The analysis is ready once the draft references are removed (issue 1). Issues 2–4 are worth a few extra sentences, but none of them changes the conclusion: there is no reliable evidence of improvement, and no case yet for a larger share of attempts.
</review>

**What the review does not change:** every figure checks out, and the conclusion and recommendation stand. I also checked the reviewer's new numbers (32.5%, 2.9 pp, 7.5 and 3.1 attempts per game) and they are correct.

# Guard X: Three-Point Shooting Since the Coaching Change

## Summary

The data do not show that X's three-point shooting genuinely improved after the change of shooting coach. They do not support giving him a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season.

His raw percentage rose from 34.0% to 40.0%, but three facts undercut that rise:

- **The gain is accounted for by weak opponents.** The rise comes entirely from 30 attempts against the league's two weakest perimeter defences, teams he did not face before game 30. Against all other opponents he shot 28% after the change, below his pre-change rate.
- **The gap is within normal variation.** Even before adjusting for opponents, a 6-point difference on these sample sizes is easily produced by chance.
- **Free throws did not improve.** His free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% to 78.6%. There is no corroborating sign of better mechanics.

The best current estimate of X's ability is somewhere between 32.5% and 36%. That is at or a little below league average.

## Data and context

- The season is split at game 30, when the new shooting coach took over. The coach works with the whole squad, not only X.
- X played all 50 games, at about 32 minutes per game in both periods. Changes in playing time therefore do not explain any difference.
- Shooting percentage = makes ÷ attempts.

| | Games 1–30 | Games 31–50 | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-point makes / attempts | 51 / 150 | 32 / 80 | 83 / 230 |
| Three-point % | 34.0% | 40.0% | 36.1% |
| Three-point attempts per game | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.6 |
| Free-throw makes / attempts | 80 / 100 | 55 / 70 | 135 / 170 |
| Free-throw % | 80.0% | 78.6% | 79.4% |

League average three-point percentage: 36%.

## 1. The headline improvement is driven by opponents

In games 31–50, 30 of X's 80 attempts came in 4 games against the two worst-ranked perimeter defences. He made 18 of them. He did not play either team in games 1–30, so the two periods faced different opposition.

| Games 31–50 | Games | Makes / attempts | % | Attempts per game |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vs two worst perimeter defences | 4 | 18 / 30 | 60.0% | 7.5 |
| vs all other opponents | 16 | 14 / 50 | 28.0% | 3.1 |
| Total | 20 | 32 / 80 | 40.0% | 4.0 |

The "all other opponents" group is the one most comparable to his games 1–30 schedule. Against it X shot 28%, which is 6 points worse than before the change, not better.

The 60% figure rests on only 30 shots over 4 games. It should not be read as his true level against weak defences. Still, the split shows that the aggregate 40% reflects the schedule, not a better shooter.

## 2. Even the raw difference is within chance

Set the opponent split aside. A rise from 34.0% (150 attempts) to 40.0% (80 attempts) has a standard error of about 6.7 percentage points. The 6-point gain is therefore less than one standard error, well within what random variation produces.

A true 36% shooter would quite often post a 34% stretch followed by a 40% stretch over samples this size. Three-point percentage needs several hundred attempts to stabilise, and the post-change sample is 80.

The 28% figure against other opponents is just as noisy, on only 50 attempts. The honest conclusion is not that X got worse. It is that, once opponents are accounted for, nothing in these data distinguishes his shooting after the change from his shooting before it.

## 3. Free throws do not suggest a change in mechanics

X's free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% (80/100) to 78.6% (55/70). On 70 attempts that change is too small to mean anything.

Free throws are a reasonable, if imperfect, check on shooting technique, because they are uncontested and taken from a fixed spot. They give no sign of a mechanical improvement.

## 4. Other points to note

**Volume and opponents.** X's attempts fell from 5.0 to 4.0 per game at the same minutes. The split shows this was not a move toward fewer, better shots:
- Against the weakest defences he took 7.5 attempts per game and shot well.
- Against everyone else he took about 3.1 per game, down from 5.0 before the change, and shot 28%.

One possible reading is that normal defences were limiting his looks. These data cannot confirm that, and they say nothing about how his efficiency would change at higher volume.

**Which baseline to plan around.** His full-season rate is 36.1%. Without the 30 attempts against the two weakest defences, it is 32.5% (65/200).
- Four of 50 games against those teams may be a normal share of the schedule.
- However, those games produced 13% of his attempts, so they carry extra weight in the season figure.
- A planning range of roughly 32.5–36% is therefore reasonable.

Either end of that range is at or below league average.

**The coach worked with the whole squad.** The team's own before-and-after three-point figures, split by opponent strength, would be a far better test of the coaching effect than one player's 80 attempts.
- If the whole team improved against comparable opponents, that would be meaningful evidence.
- If only X's numbers rose, and only against weak defences, that points to the schedule and to chance.

**Expected value.** At 36.1%, an X three is worth about 1.08 points per attempt, the same as a league-average three. At 32.5% it is about 0.98. There is no evidence that moving attempts from teammates to X would add points. That depends on how teammates compare, which these data do not show.

## Recommendation

1. **Do not increase X's share of team three-point attempts on the strength of this data.** Plan around him as a roughly league-average or slightly below-average three-point shooter (about 32.5–36%).
2. **Run the comparison that would actually answer the question.** Compare opponent-adjusted three-point percentage before and after the change, for X and for the rest of the squad. Where tracking data exist, also compare shot quality: contested versus open, and catch-and-shoot versus off-the-dribble.
3. **Keep collecting evidence.** Continue X's work with the new coach. Reassess once he has a few hundred post-change attempts against a representative range of opponents.
4. **Set a concrete decision trigger in advance.** After about 250–300 further attempts, the standard error on his percentage will be about 2.9 points.
   - Revisit his role if his opponent-adjusted rate is about 40–41% or better. That is clearly above the 36% league average.
   - Do not act on a rate of 37–38%, because that is still within noise.
   - Do not reward or penalise him on short streaks in either direction.
